title: Ristamäki and Korvola v. Finland
facts:
The applicants, born in 1969 and 1953, were respectively an editor (first applicant) and his immediate superior (second applicant) at a Finnish broadcasting company.

On 27 February 2006 the company broadcast on a national TV channel a current affairs programme criticising the lack of co-operation between the authorities in a specific investigation into economic crime. The programme revealed that the tax authorities had refused a request by the National Bureau of Investigation to conduct a tax inspection of two companies running a sports centre. It referred, inter alia, to K.U., a well-known Finnish businessman who was then standing trial for economic offences, and stated that the police wanted to know whether the sports centre had been purchased with K.U.'s money. The programme was rebroadcast the next day with an addition: K.U.'s business partner stated that the money spent on the sports centre had come from an insurance company, not from K.U.

On 10 December 2007 the public prosecutor charged both applicants, together with the company's editor-in-chief, with aggravated defamation. The charge alleged that the first applicant, by editing the programme, and the second applicant, by allowing its broadcast, had intentionally and in concert made false insinuations about K.U. that were conducive to causing him suffering, contempt and damage. K.U. claimed compensation for mental anguish and legal costs. The applicants contested the charges. They argued that all the information was correct, that there had been no false insinuation and no criminal intent, and that the programme concerned an issue of general importance, namely co-operation between the police and the tax authorities.

On 9 May 2008 the Helsinki District Court gave judgment. It found that the first applicant had edited the programme, which had reached some 750,000 viewers and had been announced as a report on the termination of tax inspections of the affairs of a person in a high position and his friend. The programme opened with footage from K.U.'s criminal trial shot that same day. This was followed by a diagram illustrated with K.U.'s photograph reading "National Bureau of Investigation → [K.U.] → [K.U.'s] business associate → Sports centre", while the narration ran:

"The Helsinki District Court continued today the examination of an extensive trial concerning economic crime. One of the accused was the businessman [K.U.], with previous convictions for economic offences. He is being charged with having concealed from his creditors millions of his assets. There are nine other defendants who have allegedly hidden [K.U.'s] assets around the world. The National Bureau of Investigation worked for years on this money laundering case, which is probably the largest of its kind in Finland. Now it has come to light that spanners were thrown into the works of the [K.U.] investigation from unexpected quarters. In 2001 one of [K.U.'s] close associates decided to invest in the sports business. He bought himself into a sports centre in Helsinki and became its managing director. The National Bureau of Investigation became interested in whose money was used in the purchase. [K.U.'s] associates' own assets would not have been sufficient to acquire the sports centre. The National Bureau of Investigation asked the tax authorities to conduct a tax inspection of the companies running the centre. The police wanted to know whether it had been purchased using [K.U.'s] money."

The court summarised the remainder of the programme as follows:

"After this a criminal inspector explains that in November 2001 the National Bureau of Investigation lodged a written request with the tax administration for tax inspection concerning two companies in the sports business and that, according to the information acquired, such inspections were not carried out. It was then noted in the programme that [this kind of omission] was very rare in the co-operation between the police and the tax authorities and that this was the only branch in the [K.U.] investigation, where the tax authorities refused to co-operate with the police. It was also mentioned in the programme that in 2001 the Uusimaa Tax Office had, at the request of the police, carried out inspections of the tax affairs of the director general for the National Board of Patents and Registration and that in these investigations the tax inspectors had [come across] the aforementioned sports centre. It was deemed that a good friend and a business associate to the director general had invested in the sports centre. In May 2001 the head of the tax inspection unit had put the brakes on the investigation into the director general's affairs and called off the inspections of the companies running the sports centre.

It was also mentioned in the programme that after the sports centre came into the possession of [K.U.'s] friend, the National Bureau of Investigation had asked the tax authorities to continue the inspections of the companies running the sports centre but nothing happened. During the investigations the director general of the National Board of Patents and Registration and the tax commissioners attempted to hinder the tax inspectors' work.

Finally, it is mentioned in the programme that if the investigation concerning the sports centre had been continued because of [K.U.], that might have again raised delicate issues concerning the friend of the director general of the National Board of Patents and Registration and the commission [he] was paid in connection with the change of office quarters of the latter. But since nothing was done, nothing was found out. In this context, the diagram with [K.U.'s] photograph was again shown."

The court found that the second applicant had read the script and authorised the broadcast. Before the rebroadcast, K.U. had contacted the first applicant and insisted that the part concerning him be removed. The second applicant and the editor-in-chief discussed this demand and decided not to accede to it. Having watched the programme, the second applicant decided that at the end of the rebroadcast the announcer would state that K.U.'s business associate submitted that the money had come from an insurance company and not from K.U. A follow-up programme on 6 March 2006 reported that the business associate had presented contracts showing that the sports centre and its debts had been purchased with a loan from an insurance company, and that, according to him, no money of K.U. had been invested.

The District Court observed that nothing suggested the information in the programme was false as such. It held:

"The District Court finds that the script of the programme and the use of the footage from the trial concerning [K.U.'s] alleged economic offences and the diagram concerning [K.U.] taken together create an impression that [K.U.] had made himself guilty of a crime by investing his assets in the sports centre business. It has not been asserted directly that [K.U.] had committed an offence. The programme was structured around [K.U.] On the above grounds the District Court finds that a false insinuation was made concerning [K.U.] in the programme broadcast on 27 and 28 February 2006, giving the impression that [he] had committed an offence by using assets concealed from his debtors for the purchase of the sports centre.

The addition made to the rebroadcast on 28 February 2006 does not exclude the false insinuation that [K.U.'s] money has ended up in sports centre business.

Defamation is only punishable where there is criminal intent. The defendants have not shown that they had strong grounds or probable reasons to believe that the false insinuation was accurate. The addition made to the rebroadcast, and the programme of 6 March 2006, indicate that [K.U.'s] money had not been used to finance the sports centre. It follows that further information concerning the insinuation had been available and it could have been verified. The defendants are responsible for the programme and the false insinuation contained therein. They must have considered it very likely that the programme contained a false insinuation aimed at [K.U.]. That insinuation concerns a serious act and sufficiently strong factual grounds are to be expected.

This kind of false insinuation implying that [K.U.] has committed an offence has been conducive to causing him suffering and damage and to subjecting him to contempt.

The exercise of freedom of expression, or the fact that [K.U.] is a public figure, does not justify the false insinuation given by the defendants.

The defendants have stressed that the programme concerned co-operation between the authorities. The District Court considers that presenting [that issue] would not have required connecting [K.U.] to the matter.

Whether the broadcast was deliberately or by chance scheduled on the same day as [K.U.'s] criminal trial is not relevant in this case.

The District Court finds that the [first and second] defendants have, in the above described manner, intentionally disparaged [K.U.'s] honour. ..."

Having regard to the nature and content of the insinuation, and to the fact that K.U. was at the time charged with a similar economic offence, the court found the defamation not aggravated. It convicted all defendants of defamation under Chapter 24, section 9(1)(1) of the Penal Code. Each applicant was sentenced to 30 day-fines, amounting to EUR 810 and EUR 1,230 respectively. The applicants were ordered, jointly and severally with the third defendant, to pay K.U. EUR 1,800 for suffering and EUR 1,500 in legal costs. The court sat with one professional judge and three lay judges; one lay judge favoured acquittal.

The applicants appealed. They argued that too little weight had been given to the accuracy of the information and that the programme focused on co-operation problems between the authorities, an issue of major public importance. They contended that the issue could not have been reported without reference to K.U., since the problems had occurred in the investigation of his very case. They also contested the findings of intent and damage. On 30 December 2008 the Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld the judgment without giving further reasons. On 16 December 2009 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Under Chapter 24, section 9 of the Penal Code, giving false information or making a false insinuation about another person that is conducive to causing damage, suffering or contempt constitutes defamation, punishable by a fine or up to six months' imprisonment. Section 10 provides for aggravated defamation where the offence is committed through the mass media.
applicantSubmissions: The conviction interfered with their freedom of expression and, although the interference had a basis in domestic law, it was not necessary in a democratic society.
It was not only the right but also the duty of the media towards citizens to disclose a problem of public interest such as the lack of cooperation between the police and the tax authorities.

The programme discussed two separate cases which had both attracted considerable publicity, and it was unusual that the tax authorities had declined the police's request to conduct a tax inspection in those cases; the programme revealed this issue.
It was undisputed that the information in the programme was true and correct.
The applicants had learned of the issue from the police themselves, a source they considered reliable; they acted in good faith and had no intention to defame.

The national courts accepted that the programme contained no allegation that K.U. was guilty of a crime, yet reached the erroneous conclusion that it contained a deliberate insinuation that he had invested funds to the detriment of his creditors.

It would not have been possible to criticise the tax authorities' conduct without introducing the two separate but linked cases, since it was precisely in those cases that cooperation between the authorities had failed.
After receiving new information about the financing of the sports centre, the applicants duly included it in the rebroadcast of the programme.
The domestic courts failed to strike a proper balance between the competing interests.
governmentSubmissions: The applicants' conviction, the fines, and the obligation to pay costs and damages to K.U. constituted an interference with their freedom of expression.
The interference had a basis in Finnish law, in particular Chapter 24, section 9 of the Penal Code, and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the private life of others.

Although the programme's general subject-matter, cooperation problems between the police and tax authorities, was a matter of public interest, the applicants were convicted not for raising that issue but for indirectly alleging that K.U. was guilty of an offence, which amounted to defamation.

A large number of people saw the programme; although the applicants could have been convicted of aggravated defamation on that account, the District Court did not find the offence aggravated as a whole.
The addition made to the rebroadcast stating that the money came from an insurance company did not make good the false insinuation made in the first broadcast.
The applicants ignored K.U.'s request to remove the parts concerning him and continued making an indirect allegation.
The applicants did not verify the facts before the first broadcast or between the two broadcasts, although they had the possibility to do so.

The programme as a whole gave the impression that K.U. was possibly guilty of a crime, and its message did not require showing K.U.'s photograph or mentioning his name; the whole programme was structured around him.
The applicants had admitted before the Court of Appeal that K.U. was not the subject of the programme but now argued the contrary before the Court.
The domestic courts properly found that the applicants must have considered it very likely that the programme contained a false insinuation aimed at K.U., and thus acted with intent.
The applicants did not seek legal advice on publishing K.U.'s name and photograph, either before the first broadcast or after K.U. contacted them.
Even though K.U. could be considered a public figure, that did not justify making a false insinuation about him.
The sanctions were modest and considerably smaller than in some previous cases, so the interference was proportionate and a fair balance was struck between the competing interests.
